mcqs.question: A team wants to track current queue depth, which can go up or down. Which metric type should they use?
options: A gauge, since it represents a value that can increase or decrease
A counter, since queue depth is always a whole number
A histogram, since queue depth needs percentile buckets
It doesn't matter, since Prometheus treats all metric types identically
mcqs.explanation: Gauges are for values that can rise or fall; counters are strictly increasing (until reset) and break rate math if used for something that decreases. Histograms are for distributions of observed values, not a single current value.

mcqs.question: Why does adding a raw user ID as a metric label risk taking down the monitoring backend?
options: Each unique label value creates a separate stored time series, so an unbounded-cardinality label can multiply stored series into the millions, exhausting memory or blowing the cost budget
User IDs are typically stored as strings, which Prometheus cannot parse
Labels are limited to exactly 4 values per metric by design
It only matters if the user ID also appears in log lines
mcqs.explanation: The mechanism is cardinality explosion: every distinct label value combination is its own time series in storage. An effectively unbounded value like a user ID can multiply series count enormously -- unrelated to string parsing, a label-count limit, or logs.

mcqs.question: Why can a service's average latency look healthy while its p99 latency is badly degraded?
options: An average collapses the whole distribution into one number, so a small fraction of very slow requests barely shifts it, while percentiles like p99 specifically show what that slow tail experiences
Averages and percentiles are mathematically required to always move together
p99 latency is only meaningful for services with fewer than 100 requests
This can only happen if the metrics backend has a bug
mcqs.explanation: Averages are dominated by the bulk of fast requests and are insensitive to a small slow tail; percentiles are defined precisely to expose that tail. There's no requirement that they move together, and this is a data-shape phenomenon, not a bug.
